blogs.title: Why we start by listening
blogs.excerpt: On letting communities set the priorities — and why it makes the work last.
blogs.author: Aquib Yazdani

children.text: Every piece of work we do begins with a conversation. Before any plan or budget, we ask the people closest to a challenge what they need, what is already working and what a good result would look like to them.
It is slower at the start. But work shaped by the people it serves is work they own — and work people own is work that lasts after any single project ends.
Listening does not stop once a project begins. We keep asking, keep adjusting, and report back on what we heard.

data.heading: Resources, support and opportunity for lasting change
body: Rising Beyond Borders (RBB) is a non-profit organization focused on empowering vulnerable communities with the resources, support and opportunities needed to pursue sustainable growth and lasting change.

Our work focuses on four program areas: Education, Health & Wellbeing, Livelihoods, and Community Support. Through these areas, RBB aims to help communities access support and opportunities that contribute to a more equitable future.

Yet access to learning is still uneven. Through this program area, Rising Beyond Borders aims to help vulnerable communities reach the learning opportunities and resources they need to thrive.

Skill-building that opens pathways to further learning and work

Awareness that helps people make informed choices about their health
Mental and emotional wellbeing as part of good health
Prevention, so that problems can be met before they grow

stories.title: When every learner has a book
stories.excerpt: Shared textbooks slow a whole class down. What changes when materials stop being the bottleneck?
stories.author: Rising Beyond Borders

children.text: Picture a lesson where one book is shared between several learners. The teacher reads the exercise aloud, copies it onto the board, and waits while it is copied again into notebooks. Half the lesson is gone before the learning starts.

Materials seem like the least interesting part of education, until they are missing. Then they decide how fast a class can move, which children keep up and how much of a teacher's skill ever reaches the room.

Asked what they need, teachers rarely ask for much: enough readers to go round, notebooks, a few things to make an idea visible. The difference is less about the objects than about the time and attention they free up.

quotes.attribution: I used to spend the first ten minutes writing the exercise on the board. Now we start.

impact: One textbook per learner in the classrooms supplied
Lesson time spent teaching rather than copying

stories.title: sewing
stories.excerpt: A working water point changes the shape of a day — most of all for the people who used to fetch water from far away.
stories.author: Aquib Y.

children.text: When a water point stops working, the change is not only in what people drink. The walk to the next source eats into the morning; children arrive late to school; water that is not safe starts to look good enough.

Repairing a pump is the easy part. Keeping it working is harder, and it depends less on engineering than on organisation: who notices the first sign of trouble, who holds the money for spare parts, who knows how to fix it.
Where a community takes on that care for itself, a water point stops being a gift that can break and becomes something people own. That is the difference between a repair and a lasting change.
It is a pattern that runs through community health work: the most valuable support is often the kind that makes outside help less necessary next time.

quotes.attribution: We keep a small fund for parts now. The last repair took an afternoon, not a month.` | `A member of the water point committee

impact: Water points repaired and maintained by their communities
Shorter walks for water for the families who fetch it

stories.title: Learning to read, together
stories.excerpt: Why a quiet hour with books, a little patience and no marks can matter as much as any lesson.
stories.author: Rising Beyond Borders

children.text: Most afternoons the room is noisier than a library should be. Children arrive straight from school, drop their bags and go looking for the book they were halfway through the day before.
Reading clubs start from a simple observation: the children who struggle to read in class are often the ones who never get to read for pleasure. Here there are no marks, and no one is in a hurry.
A volunteer reads aloud first, then steps back. Older children begin to help younger ones. A parent waiting at the door sometimes stays to listen, and leaves with a book to share at home.
The lesson for anyone planning this kind of work is that confidence comes before fluency. A child who believes reading is for them will practise; a child who does not will find reasons not to.

quotes.text: Nobody tells me to read faster here. I just read.` | `A reading club member, aged 9
quotes.attribution: I came to wait for my daughter and ended up staying for the story.

projects.title: Community Reading Clubs
projects.description: After-school reading clubs that give children regular, relaxed time with books and an encouraging adult.
context: Many children finish their first years of school still unsure of their reading. Classrooms are busy, books at home can be scarce, and a child who falls behind early often stays behind.
Reading clubs offer something simple: time, books and encouragement, away from the pressure of marks.
activities: Regular reading time in a calm, welcoming space
Books chosen for different ages and reading levels
Reading aloud, storytelling and games that build confidence
approach: Clubs are shaped with families and schools, so they fit around the school day and the languages children speak at home.
Volunteers are prepared to support reading without turning it into another lesson, and children help each other as they grow in confidence.
outcomes: Children who enjoy reading and choose to read
Families more involved in their children's learning

projects.title: Learning Materials for Classrooms
projects.description: Books, notebooks and teaching materials for classrooms that have too few — chosen with the teachers who use them.
context: When learners share one book between several, lessons slow to the pace of the page-turn. Teachers spend their time copying onto the board instead of teaching, and the children who most need help get the least of it.
activities: Materials matched to what is being taught
Guidance for teachers on using them well
Teachers better equipped to support every child
approach: Teachers decide what is needed — not a standard list chosen from far away.
Materials are sourced as close to the school as possible, and checked on later to make sure they are in use rather than in a cupboard.
outcomes: Every learner with the materials to take part
More of the lesson spent teaching
Teachers better equipped to support every child

projects.title: Teacher Mentoring Network
projects.description: Pairing newer teachers with experienced colleagues, for support through their first years in the classroom.
context: New teachers often start alone: a full classroom, little preparation time and no one to ask. Many leave the profession early — and their pupils lose a teacher just as they were getting to know them.
activities: Regular conversations between mentor and teacher
Small peer groups to share what works
Practical help with planning and inclusive teaching
approach: Mentoring is built on trust, not inspection: teachers set their own goals and decide what they want help with.
What works in one classroom is shared with others, so good practice spreads between schools.
outcomes: Teachers who feel confident and supported
Experienced teachers whose knowledge is passed on

projects.title: Community Health Days
projects.description: Open days that bring basic health checks, information and advice closer to families who live far from a clinic.
context: Distance, cost and a day's lost earnings can all delay a visit to a clinic. Small health problems go unchecked until they become serious ones.
activities: Basic health checks in a familiar community setting
Clear, practical health information
Referrals to the services people can use afterwards
approach: Health days are planned alongside the health services people already use, so they strengthen those services rather than replace them.
Checks are private and respectful, and anyone who needs more care leaves knowing where to go next.
outcomes: Families better informed about their health
Stronger links between communities and local services

body: Every partnership begins with a conversation about shared aims, what each side can bring, and how the people the work serves will have a say.

getInvolved.shortDescription: See community-focused work first-hand, on a visit planned with the people it serves.
getInvolved.hubNote: See the work first-hand on a visit planned with the communities it serves, and register your interest in a future trip.

sections.heading: Why travel with us
body: There is no better way to understand the work than to see it. Travelling with us means meeting the communities and teams behind it — on their terms, with respect for their time and privacy — and coming home able to share what you saw.

sections.heading: What a trip could involve
items: Time with program teams and the communities they work with
Learning about the local context the work happens in
Time together each day to reflect on what you have seen

sections.heading: Dates and practical details
body: Dates, costs and practical details are shared once a trip is confirmed. Register your interest below and we will let you know when trips are planned.
